title: LT1, LT2 and the threshold zoo
goal: Sort the many lactate threshold names into a two-threshold model, and explain why a fixed lactate value such as 4 mmol·L⁻¹ can mislead for an individual athlete.

steps.title: 25 names for two bends
steps.text:
A review of the literature found **25** different [lactate threshold](g:lactate-threshold) concepts. They fall into three groups: fixed lactate values; the first rise above baseline; and methods aimed at MLSS or at a sharp change in the slope of the [lactate curve](g:lactate-curve) [[c:lt-25-concepts]].

Most names point to one of two bends:

| bend | names you'll meet |
|---|---|
| first rise (LT1) | LT, LT1, [aerobic threshold](g:aerobic-threshold) |
| steep climb (LT2) | LT2, [anaerobic threshold](g:anaerobic-threshold), lactate turn point, individual anaerobic threshold, [OBLA](g:obla), [Dmax](g:dmax) |

'Anaerobic' is a leftover from an old theory. As the *Lactate* module showed, lactate rises because [glycolysis](g:glycolysis) speeds up, not because the muscle runs out of oxygen [[c:anaerobic-misnomer]].

claims.text: A review located 25 different lactate threshold concepts, which fall into three categories.

evidence.quote: A total of 25 different LT concepts were located. All concepts were divided into three categories.
The third category consists of threshold concepts that aim at detecting either the MLSS or a rapid/distinct change in the inclination of the blood lactate curve (category 3).

claims.text: A lack of oxygen in muscle is not the main reason blood lactate rises during incremental exercise.

evidence.quote: It is now recognized that insufficient O2 is not the primary basis for lactataemia.

steps.title: OBLA: one number for everyone
steps.text:
The oldest shortcut is a fixed value: the power or speed at which blood lactate reaches **4 mmol·L⁻¹**, called [OBLA](g:obla). It comes from German work of the 1970s, and in 15 runners the steady lactate at the highest sustainable speed did average about 4 mmol·L⁻¹ [[c:obla-origin]].

But lactate at MLSS ranges from about **1.5 to 7 mmol·L⁻¹** between people [[c:mlss-spread]]. The test also moves the answer: the faster the power rises in a step test, the higher the power at which 4 mmol·L⁻¹ is reached [[c:obla-protocol]]. And other factors can shift the whole curve up or down [[c:curve-factors]].

So 4 mmol·L⁻¹ is easy to read off, but for one athlete it can sit well above or below the steady-state ceiling.

claims.text: In Heck's early experiments in 15 participants, lactate stayed constant at intensities where it averaged about 4.0 ± 0.7 mmol·L⁻¹.

evidence.quote: These experiments on 15 participants revealed to us that the lactate concentration remained constant over time at intensities where the participants reached a blood lactate concentration of 4.0 ± 0.7 mmol/L from the 10th to the 25th minute of the trial

claims.text: Blood lactate at MLSS ranges from about 1.5 to almost 7 mmol·L⁻¹ between people, averaging about 3.7.

evidence.quote: a wide range of [La−]b values at MLSS has been reported for different subjects, from as low as 1.5 mM to almost 7 mM. However, the average value is ≈3.7 mM.
However, MLSSc has been reported to demonstrate a great variability between individuals (from 2-8 mmol/L) in capillary blood and not to be related to MLSSw.

claims.text: The steeper the rise in power during a step test, the higher the power at which 4 mmol·L⁻¹ is reached.

evidence.quote: Note that the steeper the increase of power over time, the higher the workload where a lactate concentration of 4 mmol.L − 1 is reached.

claims.text: Several factors besides fitness can shift overall blood lactate levels in a step test.

evidence.quote: This very global approach, however, is hindered by several factors that may influence overall lactate levels.

steps.title: Reading OBLA off two steps
steps.problem: In a step test, a runner's lactate is 3.1 mmol·L⁻¹ at 14 km·h⁻¹ and 4.9 mmol·L⁻¹ at 15 km·h⁻¹. At what speed does she reach 4 mmol·L⁻¹?
steps: Treat the curve between the two steps as a straight line (interpolation).
Go the same share of the way between the speeds: 14 + 0.5 × (15 − 14) = 14.5 km·h⁻¹.
The real curve bends upwards, so the straight line is a small approximation; small steps keep the error small.

steps.title: Reading the shape: Dmax
steps.text:
Other methods use the shape of the curve instead of one value. [Dmax](g:dmax) draws a straight line from the first to the last point of the test and takes the point of the curve farthest from that line. In 8 male cyclists tested twice a week apart, it gave values similar to established methods and repeated well [[c:dmax-reliable]].

It takes the guesswork out of 'eyeballing' a bend. But it depends on the end points: the last point is wherever the athlete stopped. Stop the test early and the line, and so the threshold, moves.

All curve methods share that weakness: the number of steps, their length and their size change the curve they are read from.

claims.text: In 8 male cyclists, the Dmax method gave thresholds similar to conventional methods and was reproducible.

evidence.quote: Thus, the Dmax method appears to be an objective and reliable method for threshold determination, which can be applied to various ventilatory or metabolic variables yet yield similar results.

steps.title: A two-threshold model
steps.text:
Sort the zoo and two bends remain, the frame of the 'aerobic–anaerobic transition': the intensity at which lactate first rises above baseline, and the highest intensity at which lactate production and removal still balance, the [MLSS](g:mlss) [[c:two-thresholds]].

On the domain map:

- **LT1** (or the gas exchange threshold) marks the moderate/heavy boundary; the evidence for this is reasonable [[c:lt1-boundary]].
- **LT2** methods aim at the heavy/severe boundary, but few of them hit it reliably; of the common methods, only critical power held up [[c:lt2-weak]].

So treat LT1 as a real boundary and any LT2 number as an estimate, and check it against how a long steady effort actually behaves.

claims.text: The aerobic–anaerobic transition can be described by two breakpoints: the first rise in lactate above baseline and the MLSS.

evidence.quote: This model consists of two typical breakpoints that are passed during incremental exercise: the intensity at which bLa begin to rise above baseline levels and the highest intensity at which lactate production and elimination are in equilibrium (maximal lactate steady state [MLSS]).

claims.text: LT1, GET and VT have some evidence for marking the moderate/heavy boundary.

evidence.quote: There is some evidence to support the validity of LT1, GET, and VT to delineate the moderate and heavy domains of exercise.

claims.text: Apart from critical power and critical speed, there is little evidence that common methods mark the heavy/severe boundary.

evidence.quote: However, there is little evidence to support the validity of most commonly used methods, with exception of CP and CS, to delineate the heavy and severe domains of exercise.

points: There are about 25 lactate threshold concepts, but most point to one of two bends: LT1 (first rise, 'aerobic threshold') and LT2 (steep climb, 'anaerobic threshold', OBLA, Dmax).
'Anaerobic threshold' is a misleading name: lactate rises because glycolysis speeds up, not because muscle lacks oxygen.
OBLA (4 mmol·L⁻¹) is easy to read off, but MLSS lactate ranges about 1.5–7 mmol·L⁻¹ and faster step tests push the 4 mmol·L⁻¹ power up.
Curve-shape methods like Dmax avoid eyeballing but depend on the test's steps and end point.
Two-threshold model: LT1 ≈ moderate/heavy boundary (reasonable evidence); LT2 methods only estimate the heavy/severe boundary.

variants.stem: A lab report gives a runner's 'aerobic threshold' and 'anaerobic threshold'. Which bends of the lactate curve do these names most likely mean?

options.text: The first rise (LT1) and the steep climb (LT2)
options.why: Right: 'aerobic threshold' is an older name for LT1 and 'anaerobic threshold' for LT2.

options.text: Two different estimates of the same bend
options.why: The two names were coined for two separate bends, one low and one high on the curve.

options.text: LT1 and the peak lactate at exhaustion
options.why: Peak lactate is the highest value reached, not a threshold; 'anaerobic threshold' means LT2.

options.text: VO₂max and the first rise in lactate
options.why: VO₂max is a maximal value, not a bend in the lactate curve.

variants.stem: Why do physiologists call the name 'anaerobic threshold' misleading?

options.text: Lactate rises from faster glycolysis, not lack of oxygen
options.why: Right: insufficient oxygen is not the main cause of the rise in blood lactate.

options.text: Blood lactate doesn't change at that intensity
options.why: Lactate does rise steeply there; the problem is the explanation in the name, not the bend.

options.text: Aerobic ATP supply stops completely above it
options.why: Aerobic supply keeps rising above LT2; it supplies most of the energy in efforts of a few minutes or more.

options.text: It only happens above VO₂max
options.why: LT2 sits well below VO₂max, typically in the upper part of the heavy domain.

variants.stem: In a step test, a cyclist's lactate is 3.2 mmol·L⁻¹ at 240 W and 4.4 mmol·L⁻¹ at 270 W. At what power does he reach 4 mmol·L⁻¹ (OBLA)?

options.why: This measures from the wrong end: (4.4 − 4) ÷ 1.2 = 0.33, added to 240 W. The fraction belongs to the distance up from the lower step.
This just takes the nearest step. OBLA lies between the two steps, so interpolate.
This scales the top step by 4 ÷ 4.4. Lactate isn't proportional to power; use the two steps on either side.

variants.stem: A runner's lactate is 3.1 mmol·L⁻¹ at 15 km·h⁻¹ and 4.6 mmol·L⁻¹ at 16 km·h⁻¹. At what speed does she reach 4 mmol·L⁻¹?

options.text: 15.6 km·h⁻¹
15.4 km·h⁻¹
options.why: This measures from the wrong end: (4.6 − 4) ÷ 1.5 = 0.4, added to 15 km·h⁻¹. The fraction belongs to the distance up from the lower step.

options.text: 16.0 km·h⁻¹
options.why: This takes the nearest step above. OBLA lies between the two steps.

options.text: 13.9 km·h⁻¹
options.why: This scales the top speed by 4 ÷ 4.6. Lactate isn't proportional to speed; interpolate between the two steps.

variants.stem: On the bike, a triathlete's lactate is 2.5 mmol·L⁻¹ at 200 W and 4.5 mmol·L⁻¹ at 225 W. At what power does she reach 4 mmol·L⁻¹?

options.why: This measures from the wrong end: (4.5 − 4) ÷ 2 = 0.25, added to 200 W.
This takes the nearest step. OBLA lies between the two steps.
This scales the top step by 4 ÷ 4.5 (= 200 W). Lactate isn't proportional to power.

variants.stem: A cyclist's MLSS, measured with 30-minute rides, comes with a lactate of only 2.4 mmol·L⁻¹. His coach sets 'threshold' intervals at his 4 mmol·L⁻¹ power from a step test. What is most likely?

options.text: The intervals sit above his MLSS and lactate keeps rising
options.why: Right: his steady-state ceiling comes at 2.4 mmol·L⁻¹, so the 4 mmol·L⁻¹ power is higher than MLSS power.

options.text: The intervals sit below his MLSS and feel easy
options.why: That would be true for someone whose MLSS lactate is above 4 mmol·L⁻¹, not 2.4.

options.text: The intervals sit exactly at his MLSS
options.why: Only if his MLSS lactate were 4 mmol·L⁻¹; it ranges about 1.5–7 between people.

options.text: The intervals sit at his first lactate threshold
options.why: LT1 is where lactate first rises above rest, usually around 1–2 mmol·L⁻¹, well below 4.

variants.stem: A runner's MLSS comes with a lactate of 6.5 mmol·L⁻¹. She sets her tempo runs at her 4 mmol·L⁻¹ speed. What is most likely?

options.text: The runs sit below her MLSS, easier than she meant
options.why: Right: she only reaches her steady-state ceiling at 6.5 mmol·L⁻¹, so 4 mmol·L⁻¹ comes at a lower speed.

options.text: The runs sit above her MLSS, so lactate keeps rising
options.why: That fits someone whose MLSS lactate is below 4 mmol·L⁻¹, not 6.5.

options.text: The runs sit exactly at her MLSS
options.why: Only if her MLSS lactate were 4 mmol·L⁻¹; hers is 6.5.

options.text: The runs sit in the severe domain
options.why: Severe starts above the steady-state ceiling; she is below it.

variants.stem: A triathlete does two step tests on the bike: one with 5-minute steps, one with 1-minute steps of the same size. Where does the 4 mmol·L⁻¹ power land in the faster test?

options.text: Higher, because blood lactate lags behind power
options.why: Right: the steeper power rises, the higher the power at which 4 mmol·L⁻¹ is reached.

options.text: Lower, because she tires sooner
options.why: A faster test ends sooner, and lactate has less time to build at each power, so the value moves up, not down.

options.text: The same, because 4 mmol·L⁻¹ is fixed
options.why: The lactate value is fixed; the power at which it appears depends on the protocol.

options.text: It can't be found with 1-minute steps
options.why: It can be read off; it just won't match a test with longer steps.

variants.stem: A runner stops a step test two stages early because she feels unwell. What happens to her Dmax threshold compared with a full test?

options.text: It probably moves lower, since the line's end point moved
options.why: Right: with the last point lower on the curve, the line is flatter and the farthest point shifts to a lower speed.

options.text: It stays the same, since Dmax uses only the first rise
options.why: Dmax uses the whole curve, including the last point; that is what makes it sensitive to the end of the test.

options.text: It moves higher, since fewer points are averaged
options.why: Dmax doesn't average points; the farthest point moves down, not up, when the curve is cut short.

options.text: It can't be found without a lactate at exhaustion
options.why: Dmax uses the last point reached, whatever it is; the problem is that the answer changes.

variants.stem: A lab report gives a cyclist LT1 = 190 W and 'LT2' = 265 W, the second from a fixed 4 mmol·L⁻¹. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: 190 W marks moderate/heavy; 265 W only estimates heavy/severe
options.why: Right: LT1 has reasonable evidence as the moderate/heavy boundary; fixed-value LT2s are rough estimates of the heavy/severe boundary.

options.text: 265 W is exactly his critical power
options.why: Few LT2 methods match CP; a fixed 4 mmol·L⁻¹ can sit well above or below it.

options.text: Both are exact domain boundaries
options.why: Only LT1 (or GET) has good support as a boundary; LT2 methods are estimates.

options.text: Neither relates to the intensity domains
options.why: LT1 is one of the accepted markers of the moderate/heavy boundary.

variants.stem: Most studies in a review found strong correlations between lactate thresholds and endurance performance. Why doesn't that alone show a threshold method is good for setting one athlete's training power?

options.text: A strong correlation can hide large individual errors
options.why: Right: thresholds can rank people well and still miss one person's MLSS by a lot; the review notes these individual differences are rarely reported.

options.text: Correlations below 0.95 mean nothing
options.why: Strong correlations do mean something: they show the threshold ranks athletes well. The issue is the error for one person.

options.text: Correlations prove the threshold causes performance
options.why: Correlation doesn't show cause, and cause isn't the question here: accuracy for one athlete is.

options.text: Correlations only hold for running events
options.why: They were strongest in running, but the problem with individual accuracy applies to any sport.
